title: Nobel disease
content_html:
From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Nobel disease or Nobelitis is an informal term for the embrace of strange or scientifically unsound ideas by some Nobel Prize winners, usually later in life.[1][2][3] It has been argued that the effect results, in part, from a tendency for Nobel winners to feel empowered by the award to speak on topics outside their specific area of expertise,[4][5] although it is unknown whether Nobel Prize winners are more prone to this tendency than other individuals.[6] Paul Nurse, co-winner of the 2001 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, warned later laureates against "believing you are expert in almost everything, and being prepared to express opinions about most issues with great confidence, sheltering behind the authority that the Nobel Prize can give you". Nurse also noted the media's role in reinforcing this tendency, observing that after receiving his Nobel Prize, journalists had begun to take him seriously when he commented on issues about which he knew little.[7]

While it remains unclear whether Nobel winners are statistically more prone to critical thinking errors than other scientists, the phenomenon provides an existence proof that being an authority in one field does not necessarily make one an authority in any other field, and, to the extent that winning a Nobel Prize serves as a proxy indicator of scientific brilliance and high general intelligence, such characteristics are not incompatible with irrationality.[8][6]

Nobel disease demonstrates that, for some prize winners, being universally hailed as correct appears to bolster the individual laureate's confirmation bias more than it does their skepticism.[9] Milton Friedman, winner of the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences in 1976, said this of the Nobel disease as it relates to his economic thinking towards an "antidote":[10]

I myself have been asked my opinion on everything from a cure for the common cold to the market value of a letter signed by John F. Kennedy. Needless to say the attention [from receiving a Nobel prize] is flattering, but also corrupting. Somehow we badly need an antidote for both the inflated attention granted a Nobel laureate in areas outside his competence and the inflated ego each of us is in danger of acquiring. My own field suggests one obvious antidote: competition through the establishment of many more awards. But a product that has been so successful is not easy to replace. Hence, I suspect that our inflated egos are safe for a good long time to come.[10]

Winners reported as examples

[edit]

Phillip Lenard won the 1905 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on cathode rays. He was a supporter of the Nazi party, and promoted the idea of Deutsche Physik and Jewish physics.[8]

Alexis Carrel, winner of the 1912 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the invention of the perfusion pump, became an advocate of eugenic policies in Vichy France.[8]

Charles Richet won the 1913 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on anaphylaxis. He also believed in extrasensory perception, paranormal activity, dowsing, and ghosts.[6]

Linus Pauling won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on chemical bonds and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his peace activism. A decade before winning the first prize, he was diagnosed with Bright's disease, which he treated in part by ingesting vitamin supplements, which he claimed dramatically improved his condition. He later espoused taking high doses of vitamin C to reduce the likelihood and severity of experiencing the common cold. Pauling himself consumed amounts of vitamin C on a daily basis that were more than 120 times the recommended daily intake. He further argued that megadoses of vitamin C have therapeutic value for treating schizophrenia and for prolonging cancer patients' lives. These claims are not supported by the best available science.[8][1][2]

William Shockley, who shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics with Walter Houser Brattain and John Bardeen for their invention of the point-contact transistor, believed in racialism and eugenics.[4][8]

James Watson was awarded the 1962 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, together with Francis Crick and Maurice Wilkins, "for their discoveries concerning the molecular structure of nucleic acids and its significance for information transfer in living material". Since at least 2000, Watson consistently and publicly claimed that black people are on average less intelligent than white people, and that exposure to sunlight in tropical regions and higher levels of melanin cause dark-skinned people to have a higher sex drive.[8][11][12]

Nikolaas Tinbergen won the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discoveries concerning the organization and elicitation of individual and social behavior patterns in animals. During his Nobel acceptance speech, Tinbergen promoted the widely discredited[13] "refrigerator mother" hypothesis of the causation of autism. In 1985, Tinbergen coauthored a book with his wife[14] that recommended the use of "holding therapy" for autism, a form of treatment that is empirically unsupported and that can be physically dangerous.[1][8]

Brian Josephson won the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1973 for his prediction of the Josephson effect. Josephson has promoted a number of scientifically unsupported or discredited beliefs, including the homeopathic notion that water can somehow "remember" the chemical properties of substances diluted within it (cf. § Luc Montagnier); the view that transcendental meditation is helpful for bringing unconscious traumatic memories into conscious awareness; and the possibility that humans can communicate with each other by telepathy.[8]

Kary Mullis won the 1993 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for development of the polymerase chain reaction. Mullis disagreed with the scientifically accepted view that AIDS is caused by HIV, claiming that the virus is barely detectable in people with the disease. He also expressed doubt in the evidence for human-caused climate change. In his autobiography, Mullis professed a belief in astrology and wrote about an encounter with a fluorescent, talking raccoon that he suggested might have been an extraterrestrial alien.[4][8]

Louis J. Ignarro was one of three winners of the 1998 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for his research on nitric oxide as a signaling molecule in the cardiovascular system, which led to the development of new medications to treat cardiovascular disease, as well as of Viagra. In 2003, he became a consultant for Herbalife (which has been investigated for various kinds of dishonesty about its products). As a member of their Scientific Advisory Board, he helped to promote dubious dietary supplements. He studied the effects of his pet invention, Niteworks, on mice, and is known for saying, "What's good for mice is good for humans," an unverified statement.[8]

Luc Montagnier co-discovered HIV in 1983, for which he won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 2009, in a non-peer-reviewed paper in a journal that he had founded, Montagnier claimed that solutions containing the DNA of pathogenic bacteria and viruses could emit low frequency radio waves that induce surrounding water molecules to become arranged into "nanostructures". He suggested water could retain such properties even after the original solutions were massively diluted, to the point where the original DNA had effectively vanished, and that water could retain the "memory" of substances with which it had been in contact – claims that place his work in close alignment with the pseudoscientific tenets of homeopathy (cf. § Brian Josephson). He further claimed that DNA sequence information could be "teleported" to a separate test tube of purified water via these radio waves. He explained this in the framework of quantum field theory.[15][2][16] He supported the scientifically discredited view that vaccines cause autism and has claimed that antibiotics are of therapeutic value in the treatment of autism.[8] During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier promoted the idea that SARS-CoV-2 was deliberately created and escaped from a laboratory,[17][18] a claim which has been rejected by other virologists.[19]

Scott O. Lilienfeld et al. list more examples of "Nobel laureates who held/hold weird ideas": Pierre Curie, who participated in spiritual seances; John William Strutt, who "was fond of parapsychology"; J. J. Thomson, who was interested in psychic phenomena; Santiago Ramón y Cajal, who wrote a book "on hypnosis, spiritualism, and metaphysics"; Wolfgang Pauli, who, together with Carl Jung, "developed the concept of synchronicity"; Egas Moniz, for his belief that lobotomy can treat mental illnesses; Julian Schwinger, for his work on cold fusion; Ivar Giaever, for global warming skepticism; Arthur Schawlow, for his support of a subsequently debunked "technique of facilitated communication for autism"; and Richard Smalley, for promotion of anti-evolutionary ideas.[20]

blocks.html_en: Linus Pauling won the 1954 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for his work on chemical bonds and the Nobel Peace Prize in 1962 for his peace activism. A decade before winning the first prize, he was diagnosed with Bright's disease, which he treated in part by ingesting vitamin supplements, which he claimed dramatically improved his condition. He later espoused taking high doses of vitamin C to reduce the likelihood and severity of experiencing the common cold. Pauling himself consumed amounts of vitamin C on a daily basis that were more than 120 times the recommended daily intake. He further argued that megadoses of vitamin C have therapeutic value for treating schizophrenia and for prolonging cancer patients' lives. These claims are not supported by the best available science.[8][1][2]

blocks.html_en: Luc Montagnier co-discovered HIV in 1983, for which he won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 2009, in a non-peer-reviewed paper in a journal that he had founded, Montagnier claimed that solutions containing the DNA of pathogenic bacteria and viruses could emit low frequency radio waves that induce surrounding water molecules to become arranged into "nanostructures". He suggested water could retain such properties even after the original solutions were massively diluted, to the point where the original DNA had effectively vanished, and that water could retain the "memory" of substances with which it had been in contact – claims that place his work in close alignment with the pseudoscientific tenets of homeopathy (cf. § Brian Josephson). He further claimed that DNA sequence information could be "teleported" to a separate test tube of purified water via these radio waves. He explained this in the framework of quantum field theory.[15][2][16] He supported the scientifically discredited view that vaccines cause autism and has claimed that antibiotics are of therapeutic value in the treatment of autism.[8] During the COVID-19 pandemic, Montagnier promoted the idea that SARS-CoV-2 was deliberately created and escaped from a laboratory,[17][18] a claim which has been rejected by other virologists.[19]

来自免费百科全书维基百科

诺贝尔病或诺贝尔炎是一个非正式术语，指一些诺贝尔奖获得者通常在晚年接受奇怪或科学上不合理的想法。[1][2][3]有人认为，这种效应在一定程度上是由于诺贝尔奖获得者倾向于认为该奖项赋予他们就其特定专业领域之外的话题发表演讲的倾向，[4][5]，尽管尚不清楚诺贝尔奖获得者是否比其他人更容易出现这种倾向。[6] 2001 年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖共同获得者保罗·纳斯 (Paul Nurse) 警告后来的获奖者，不要“相信自己几乎在所有事情上都是专家，并准备好以极大的信心就大多数问题表达观点，以诺贝尔奖所赋予的权威为掩护”。 纳斯还指出了媒体在强化这种趋势方面的作用，他观察到，在获得诺贝尔奖后，当他评论他知之甚少的问题时，记者们开始认真对待他。 [7]

虽然尚不清楚诺贝尔奖获得者在统计上是否比其他科学家更容易出现批判性思维错误，但这一现象提供了一个存在证据，即在一个领域成为权威并不一定会使一个人在任何其他领域成为权威，而且，就获得诺贝尔奖作为科学才华和高智力的代理指标而言，这些特征与非理性并非不相容。 [8][6]

诺贝尔病表明，对于一些获奖者来说，被普遍认为是正确的似乎更能增强获奖者个人的确认偏见，而不是他们的怀疑主义。 [9] 1976年诺贝尔经济学奖获得者米尔顿·弗里德曼这样评价诺贝尔病，因为这与他对“解药”的经济思考有关：[10]

我本人也曾被问过对各种事情的看法，从普通感冒的治疗方法到约翰·肯尼迪签署的一封信的市场价值。 肯尼迪. 不用说，[获得诺贝尔奖]受到的关注是令人受宠若惊的，但也具有腐败性。 不知何故，我们迫切需要一种解药，既可以缓解诺贝尔奖获得者在其能力范围之外的领域所受到的过度关注，也可以缓解我们每个人都面临的膨胀自我的危险。 我自己的领域提出了一种明显的解药：通过设立更多奖项进行竞争。 但如此成功的产品并不容易被取代。 因此，我怀疑我们膨胀的自我在未来很长一段时间内都是安全的。 [10]

获奖者作为例子报告

[edit]

菲利普·莱纳德 (Phillip Lenard) 因其在阴极射线方面的工作而获得 1905 年诺贝尔物理学奖。 他是纳粹党的支持者，并提倡德国物理学和犹太物理学的思想。 [8]

亚历克西斯·卡雷尔 (Alexis Carrel) 因发明灌注泵而获得 1912 年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖，成为维希法国优生政策的倡导者。 [8]

Charles Richet 因其对过敏反应的研究而获得 1913 年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖。 他还相信超感官知觉、超自然活动、占卜和鬼魂。 [6]

莱纳斯·鲍林因其在化学键方面的工作而获得 1954 年诺贝尔化学奖，并因其和平行动主义而获得 1962 年诺贝尔和平奖。 在获得一等奖的十年前，他被诊断出患有布莱特氏病，他通过服用维生素补充剂来部分治疗这种疾病，他声称这极大地改善了他的病情。 后来他主张服用高剂量的维生素 C 以降低患普通感冒的可能性和严重程度。 鲍林本人每天摄入的维生素 C 量是每日推荐摄入量的 120 倍以上。 他进一步指出，大剂量的维生素 C 对于治疗精神分裂症和延长癌症患者的生命具有治疗价值。 这些说法没有得到现有最佳科学的支持。[8][1][2]

威廉·肖克利 (William Shockley) 因发明点接触晶体管而与沃尔特·豪瑟·布拉顿 (Walter Houser Brattain) 和约翰·巴丁 (John Bardeen) 共同获得 1956 年诺贝尔物理学奖，他相信种族主义和优生学。 [4][8]

詹姆斯·沃森 (James Watson) 与弗朗西斯·克里克 (Francis Crick) 和莫里斯·威尔金斯 (Maurice Wilkins) 一起荣获 1962 年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖，“表彰他们在核酸分子结构及其对生命物质信息传递的重要性方面的发现”。 至少自 2000 年以来，沃森一直公开声称黑人的平均智力低于白人，而暴露在热带地区的阳光和较高水平的黑色素会导致深色皮肤的人具有更高的性欲。 [8][11][12]

尼古拉斯·丁伯根 (Nikolaas Tinbergen) 因在动物个体和社会行为模式的组织和引发方面的发现而获得 1973 年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖。 在他的诺贝尔奖获奖感言中，丁伯根提出了广受质疑的[13]自闭症因果关系的“冰箱妈妈”假说。 1985 年，Tinbergen 与妻子共同撰写了一本书[14]，建议对自闭症使用“保持疗法”，这种治疗形式在经验上不受支持，并且可能对身体造成危险。[1][8]

布莱恩·约瑟夫森 (Brian Josephson) 因预言约瑟夫森效应而获得 1973 年诺贝尔物理学奖。 约瑟夫森宣扬了许多未经科学支持或不可信的信念，包括顺势疗法的观念，即水可以以某种方式“记住”稀释在其中的物质的化学性质（参见 § 吕克·蒙塔尼耶）；超验冥想有助于将无意识的创伤记忆带入意识意识；以及人类可以通过心灵感应相互交流的可能性。 [8]

卡里·穆利斯 (Kary Mullis) 因开发聚合酶链式反应而获得 1993 年诺贝尔化学奖。 穆利斯不同意科学上公认的艾滋病是由艾滋病毒引起的观点，他声称在患有这种疾病的人身上几乎检测不到这种病毒。 他还对人为造成气候变化的证据表示怀疑。 在他的自传中，穆利斯宣称自己相信占星术，并写到了他与一只会说话的荧光浣熊的遭遇，他认为浣熊可能是外星外星人。 [4][8]

路易斯·J。 伊格纳罗因其对一氧化氮作为心血管系统信号分子的研究而成为 1998 年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖的三位获得者之一，该研究导致了治疗心血管疾病的新药物以及伟哥的开发。 2003年，他成为康宝莱（该公司因其产品的各种不诚实行为而受到调查）的顾问。 作为其科学顾问委员会的成员，他帮助推广可疑的膳食补充剂。 他研究了他的宠物发明 Niteworks 对老鼠的影响，并以“对老鼠有益的东西对人类也有好处”而闻名，这是一个未经证实的说法。 [8]

1983年，吕克·蒙塔尼（Luc Montagnier）与人共同发现了艾滋病毒，并因此获得了2008年诺贝尔生理学或医学奖。 2009年，蒙塔尼在他创办的期刊上发表的一篇未经同行评审的论文中声称，含有病原细菌和病毒DNA的溶液可以发射低频无线电波，诱导周围的水分子排列成“纳米结构”。 他认为，即使原始溶液被大量稀释，原始 DNA 已有效消失，水仍可以保留这些特性，并且水可以保留与其接触过的物质的“记忆”——这一主张使他的工作与顺势疗法的伪科学原则紧密结合（参见 § 布莱恩·约瑟夫森）。 他进一步声称，DNA 序列信息可以通过这些无线电波“传送”到一个单独的纯净水试管中。 他在量子场论的框架下解释了这一点。[15][2][16]他支持疫苗导致自闭症的科学观点，并声称抗生素在治疗自闭症方面具有治疗价值。 [8]在 COVID-19 大流行期间，蒙塔尼提出了 SARS-CoV-2 是故意制造并从实验室逃脱的观点，[17][18]这一说法已被其他病毒学家拒绝。[19]

斯科特·O. 利林菲尔德等人。列出更多“持有/持有怪异想法的诺贝尔奖得主”的例子：皮埃尔·居里，参加过精神降神会；约翰·威廉·斯特拉特（John William Strutt），“喜欢超心理学”； J。 J。 汤姆森，对心灵现象感兴趣；圣地亚哥·拉蒙·卡哈尔（Santiago Ramón y Cajal），写了一本“关于催眠、招魂术和形而上学”的书；沃尔夫冈·泡利 (Wolfgang Pauli) 与卡尔·荣格 (Carl Jung) 一起“提出了同步性的概念”； Egas Moniz，因为他相信脑叶白质切除术可以治疗精神疾病；朱利安·施温格 (Julian Schwinger)，因其在冷聚变方面的工作； Ivar Giaever，对全球变暖持怀疑态度；亚瑟·肖洛 (Arthur Schawlow)，支持后来被揭穿的“自闭症促进沟通技术”；和理查德·斯莫利（Richard Smalley），促进反进化思想。 [20]
